walkthroughs.body_html:
Criminal Psychology — a core area of GCSE Psychology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Criminal Psychology brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Criminal Psychology.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Eysenck's theory”?
options: Criminals score high on extraversion, neuroticism and psychoticism (E, N, P); inherited nervous system underactivity.
Canter's UK approach: statistical analysis of crime scene data to derive profiles; investigative psychology.
Lombroso's (1876) outdated theory that criminals are evolutionary throwbacks identifiable by physical features.
FBI approach (Ressler 1986): classify crime scene as organised or disorganised to infer offender characteristics.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Bottom-up profiling”?
options: Criminals score high on extraversion, neuroticism and psychoticism (E, N, P); inherited nervous system underactivity.
Canter's UK approach: statistical analysis of crime scene data to derive profiles; investigative psychology.
Sutherland (1939): criminal behaviour learned from associates whose pro-crime attitudes outweigh anti-crime ones.
Imprisonment aims to deter, rehabilitate, incapacitate and protect; UK recidivism around 48% within one year.
